content: I'm a complete novice at this. What actually makes bread rise? I thought yeast and baking soda were basically the same thing: both make bubbles when they get wet, and those bubbles push the dough upward. Is that the whole process?

Both can create carbon dioxide bubbles, but they do it differently. Yeast is alive: it consumes sugars from the dough and releases carbon dioxide over time. Baking soda is a chemical that releases carbon dioxide when it meets enough acid and moisture. The gas expands the dough, but bread also needs a stretchy structure that can trap those bubbles rather than letting them escape.

If yeast is alive, what is it eating in plain bread dough? Flour does not taste sugary to me, so I assumed the yeast mostly reacts with water. Why does a recipe sometimes add sugar if flour already works?

Water wakes the yeast and lets reactions occur, but it is not the food. Flour contains starch, and enzymes in the flour break some of that starch into smaller sugars yeast can consume. Added sugar provides an immediately available food source, so fermentation may begin faster. Too much sugar can actually slow yeast by drawing water away from its cells.

So the gas is carbon dioxide, but why does it stay inside the dough instead of drifting away like bubbles from a fizzy drink? Is the dough simply thick enough, or does something in the flour make actual little containers?

Proteins in wheat flour link together when flour is mixed with water, forming a stretchy network called gluten. That network surrounds many tiny pockets of gas. Dough thickness helps slow the bubbles, but gluten is the main flexible framework that holds them. During rising, bubbles enlarge and the dough stretches; without enough structure, the gas escapes or the dough collapses.

What changes when the loaf enters the oven? I had pictured the yeast continuing to make more and more gas until the bread is done. Does the heat speed it up, stop it, or make the existing bubbles larger?

At first, warming briefly speeds yeast activity, while existing gas expands and some water turns to steam. This produces the final rapid swelling called oven spring. As the loaf gets hotter, the yeast dies and gas production stops. Meanwhile, starch firms up and gluten sets, changing the soft bubble walls into a stable crumb that keeps the loaf from shrinking again.

I'm a beginner with this subject. Why does kneading make bread rise better? I am fairly sure kneading works by folding extra air into the dough, almost like beating eggs, so more kneading should always produce a taller loaf. What am I missing?

Kneading may introduce a little air, but that is not its main job. It arranges and links flour proteins into a stronger gluten network. Yeast later supplies most of the gas, and the developed gluten traps it. More kneading is not always better: too little leaves weak dough, while excessive machine kneading can overheat or damage the network.

What does that network look like in ordinary terms? I picture threads tangled through the dough, but I do not understand why pushing and stretching would connect them. Does water create the threads first, with kneading only lining them up?

Threads are a useful picture. When water moistens flour, two main proteins become mobile and begin interacting. Mixing brings them into contact; repeated folding and stretching helps them form a continuous web. Some parts give strength, while others let the web extend. The result resembles a flexible net more than separate sealed bags, with gas pockets pressing against it.
Why do some recipes avoid kneading and simply leave a wet dough overnight? If kneading builds the net, it seems that an untouched dough should stay weak and let all the gas leak out before morning.

Time can do part of the same work. In a wet dough, proteins move and link while the dough rests, and occasional folds organize the developing network with little effort. Fermentation also changes the dough gradually. A no-knead recipe balances water, time, and yeast so structure develops before too much gas accumulates; untouched does not mean chemically inactive.

How can I tell whether the dough has enough of this structure without knowing what the proteins are doing? Is doubling in size proof that kneading worked, or could a weak dough also become large for a while?

Doubling shows that gas was produced and retained temporarily, but it does not prove the structure is ideal. A weak dough can inflate and then spread or collapse. A common check is to stretch a small piece gently: developed dough can form a thin, partly translucent sheet before tearing. Its overall shape and elasticity also matter, especially after a fold.

Then why does dough sometimes spring back when I shape it, while other dough stays wherever it is placed? I had treated springiness as trapped air pushing outward, but is that actually the gluten pulling the dough back?

Much of that springiness comes from the gluten network, not from air pressure alone. Stretching pulls the network out of its preferred arrangement, so it tends to recoil. A rest period lets stresses relax, making shaping easier. Dough that never springs back may be underdeveloped, very relaxed, unusually wet, or weakened by fermentation, so the surrounding clues are important.

I'm a total novice about bread making. Why does dough rise quickly on some days and barely move on others? I know warmth matters somehow, but I vaguely assumed a hotter room simply makes bigger bubbles rather than changing what the yeast does.

Warmth mainly changes how quickly yeast ferments sugars and produces carbon dioxide. Within a comfortable range, warmer dough rises faster; cold dough rises slowly. Heat also expands gas slightly, but that is a smaller part of room-temperature proofing. If dough becomes too hot, yeast is stressed or killed, so increasing temperature eventually reduces rising instead of accelerating it.

What is the yeast doing during a slow rise in the refrigerator, then? If it is almost inactive, why do recipes claim the bread tastes different after a night there instead of merely taking longer to reach the same size?

Yeast works much more slowly in the refrigerator, but it usually does not stop completely. Meanwhile, flour enzymes keep breaking larger molecules into smaller sugars, and fermentation produces acids, alcohols, and aroma compounds. Extra time allows those products to accumulate and interact. The dough therefore develops flavor as well as gas, even if its visible growth is modest.
Why does salt slow the rise? I thought salt was included only for taste, and it seems too dry and grainy to affect tiny living things once it is scattered through a large lump of wet dough.

Dissolved salt spreads through the dough water, so yeast cells encounter it even though the original crystals disappear. Salt draws water and makes it harder for yeast to function rapidly, which slows fermentation. It also strengthens the gluten network and improves flavor. Bakers use that slowing effect deliberately because steadier gas production can make timing and dough structure easier to control.

Does adding more yeast solve a dough that rises too slowly, or does it change the bread in some other way? I would expect twice as much yeast to mean exactly twice as much gas and therefore twice the loaf height.

More yeast usually shortens the time needed to produce a given amount of gas, but it does not guarantee a proportionally taller loaf. Height is limited by available food, fermentation time, dough strength, shaping, and the point at which the structure begins to fail. A large dose can make timing harder and may produce a strong yeast flavor without improving the final volume.
What does it mean when a recipe says the dough is overproofed? The word sounds as if the yeast made too much gas, but could I just press the extra bubbles out and wait for a better-sized rise again?

Overproofed dough has expanded beyond the point where its structure can reliably hold more gas. The gluten has been stretched and may also have weakened over time, while the yeast has used some of its available food. Gently pressing and reshaping can rescue mildly overproofed dough, but a severely weakened dough may not recover enough strength for a tall final rise.

Why is the finger-poke test supposed to show that point? I understand the instruction to press the dough, but not why a dent that returns slowly means it is ready while a fast return means it needs longer.

The test gives a rough sense of how stretched and relaxed the dough has become. Early in proofing, the gluten network is still tight and elastic, so it pushes a dent back quickly. Near readiness, the expanded network recovers more slowly. If the dent remains completely and the dough feels fragile, the structure may be near its limit. It is a guide, not an exact measurement.

I'm entirely new to the chemistry here. What decides whether bread keeps its risen shape or sinks? I had assumed that once yeast makes enough bubbles, the loaf is permanently larger, so a collapse after rising seems as though the bubbles somehow vanished.

A risen dough is more like an inflated soft framework than a finished solid. Its bubbles remain under pressure, and their thin walls can stretch, leak, or tear. The loaf keeps its shape only after oven heat sets the starch and proteins around those bubbles. Before that happens, weak structure, excessive expansion, or rough handling can let gas escape and cause collapse.

Why can a loaf still sink in the oven if heat is supposed to make the walls solid? I would think the outside crust hardens first and acts like a shell that holds everything upright from that point onward.

The inside must set too, and that takes longer than surface browning. Early in baking, gas expands while the crumb is still soft. If the bubble walls are too weak, they can rupture before starch and proteins firm them. A crust that sets unusually early may even restrict expansion rather than support it, leaving the interior unable to establish a stable structure.
Is that why recipes warn against opening the oven door? I have heard that cold air makes bread fall, but the loaf seems far too large for a short draft to cool its middle very much.

A brief opening may not cool the center dramatically, but it lowers oven temperature and can delay the moment when the crumb sets. That matters most while the loaf is still fragile and expanding. Movement can also disturb a very delicate structure. Once the interior has firmed, opening the door is much less likely to cause a collapse.
What part does steam play in rising? I see people add water to an oven, and I cannot tell whether the steam enters the dough to make new bubbles or simply keeps the surface wet.

Most added oven steam acts on the surface rather than entering the loaf to create new internal bubbles. It delays crust drying, so the outside stays flexible while the dough undergoes oven spring. Steam can also help produce a thin, glossy crust. Inside the loaf, water already in the dough becomes vapor and contributes to expansion of existing pockets.

Would baking soda prevent collapse better than yeast because its bubbles appear during baking? I still think of the two as interchangeable bubble makers, except that baking soda seems timed closer to when the bread becomes solid.

Baking soda does not automatically prevent collapse. It can release gas quickly when acid and moisture are present, but that gas still needs a structure able to retain it. Yeast fermentation is slower and also changes flavor and dough behavior. Recipes balance the gas source with their structure: gluten often supports yeast breads, while cakes and quick breads rely more on eggs, starch, and careful mixing.

Why do quick breads usually go into the oven soon after mixing, while yeast dough can sit for hours? If both need time for bubbles to expand, I would expect waiting to help either kind become lighter.

Chemical leaveners often begin releasing gas as soon as wet ingredients meet, so waiting can let bubbles escape before heat sets the batter. Some baking powder has a second heat-triggered stage, but prompt baking still protects the first gas. Yeast produces gas gradually and can keep replenishing it, so dough is intentionally given time to ferment and stretch before baking.
What makes large holes in one loaf and a fine, even texture in another? Is that mostly the amount of gas, or do the bubble walls combine and rearrange before the oven fixes them in place?

Both gas quantity and bubble behavior matter. Water content, gluten strength, fermentation, and handling affect whether small bubbles stay separate or merge into larger pockets. Gentle handling can preserve irregular openings, while firm pressing and tight shaping redistribute gas into many smaller cells. The oven then enlarges those cells and sets their walls, preserving much of the pattern established beforehand.
